lesson.title: IF this, THEN that
lesson.subtitle: Rules that let a device decide on its own

video.title: IF this, THEN that
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Joseph — computer studies teacher, the student's teacher (main character)
Ms Salma — maths teacher, the student's teacher (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, talking to the student)

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph unlocks an empty classroom on a Monday morning; the ceiling fan is still spinning.
scenes.animation: Fan blades spin; a calendar flips from Friday to Monday.
scenes.narration: Last term, our classroom fan ran all weekend, with nobody in the room. Someone forgot to switch it off. A small sensor with one good rule would never forget. Today, you'll write that rule.

scenes.visual: Darsi title card with the IoT track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: IF this, THEN that, the rules that let a device decide on its own.

scenes.visual: A thermometer reads 31; an IF box lights up; a THEN box switches a fan on.
scenes.animation: Each box lights in turn, joined by arrows.
scenes.narration: A device that acts on its own follows rules, each with two parts. The IF part is a condition a sensor can check: the room is above thirty degrees. The THEN part is an action: switch the fan on.

scenes.visual: Two quick shots: a school water tank with its pump, then a street light switching on at dusk.
scenes.animation: Each shot slides in as it is named.
scenes.narration: You live with rules like these. IF the water tank is low, THEN the pump starts. IF it gets dark, THEN the street light comes on.

scenes.visual: The school garden at dawn: a soil sensor in a dry bed, a clock showing 6:00, a drip line starting.
scenes.animation: Both conditions tick green, then the water flows; at noon the sun blazes and the tap stays shut.
scenes.narration: One condition is often not enough. IF the garden soil is dry AND it's early morning, THEN water it. With AND, both must be true, so at midday the pump waits, and less water dries up in the sun.

scenes.visual: A school corridor: a smoke sensor on the ceiling and a red fire button on the wall, both wired to a bell.
scenes.animation: Smoke drifts up and the bell rings; then a hand presses the button and it rings again.
scenes.narration: OR works the other way: either condition is enough. IF the smoke sensor detects smoke OR someone presses the fire button, THEN the alarm rings.

scenes.visual: Ms Salma by the school gate at dusk, pointing at the lamp above it. Two rule cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! The school gate light should come on only for people arriving after dark. Which rule does that?

scenes.visual: Split screen: the AND gate light glows only as a parent walks up at night; the OR light burns all night and flicks on at noon.
scenes.animation: Day and night cycle on both sides.
scenes.narration: AND. It must be dark, and someone must be there. With OR, the light would burn all night, and flash on at noon whenever someone walked past.

scenes.visual: A line chart of the classroom's temperature from 7:00 to 17:00 draws itself; a clock hand sweeps along it.
scenes.animation: The line draws left to right as each time is said.
scenes.on_screen_text: Test it through a whole day
scenes.narration: A rule that looks right on paper can still go wrong, so test it through a whole day. At seven, the room is cool and empty. After lunch, it's hottest. At five, everyone has gone home, but it's still warm.

scenes.visual: An empty classroom at 17:00 with the fan spinning; a second condition card snaps onto the rule and the fan stops.
scenes.animation: The card clicks into place; the fan slows to a stop.
scenes.on_screen_text: Find the fault, then fix it
scenes.narration: Now look for trouble. The rule says: IF above thirty degrees, THEN fan on. At five, it's still thirty-one degrees, so the fan runs all evening for nobody. Add AND a class is in, and it stops when everyone leaves.

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph beside a classroom window flung open in a storm, rain on the desks. Two fix cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Rain streaks; cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. A rule says: IF above thirty degrees, THEN open the window. In your test, a storm comes at two, and rain pours onto the desks. What's the best fix?

scenes.visual: Four cards line up: IF/THEN, AND, OR, a clock.
scenes.animation: Cards line up left to right, 250 ms apart.
scenes.narration: Add AND it isn't raining, so the window opens only when it's hot and dry. Remember: IF a condition, THEN an action. AND needs both; OR needs either one. And test every rule through a day.

scenes.visual: A student at a desk writes three IF/THEN rules in a notebook, with a timeline of the day drawn under them.
scenes.animation: Each rule writes itself; a red tick and a fix appear on one.
scenes.narration: Try it this week, at school or at home: write three rules for things around you, like a fan, a light or a water tank. Play each one through a day on paper, hour by hour. Find one that goes wrong, and fix it with AND or OR. Next time: when should it switch?

checkpoints.prompt: The gate light should come on only for people arriving after dark. Which rule?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — with AND, both must be true: it's dark, and someone is there.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — with OR, the light would burn all night, and flash on in daylight whenever someone walked past.

checkpoints.prompt: A rule opens the window above 30 °C, even in a rainstorm. What's the best fix?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — with AND, the window opens only when it's hot and dry.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — with OR, it would still open in a hot storm, and on every dry day, even a cold one. Both must be true, so it's AND.
